prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Startled, Somewhere, Any

outputs.L1:
Startled from its snow-day slumber by a neighbor's mutt, it knocked its buzzard's head, then could not solve the puzzle of the white pine's limbs with wings nearly too broad for any planned descent. Somewhere an awkward angel knows whether it was dead before it struck the ground. Any sinner could tell it was dead after—eyes unseen beneath bare and wrinkled lids, feet drawn up almost as high as hands. I loved to watch thistle and millet vanish beneath it in the yard.

As snow settles over feathers that will still be iridescent come spring, I recall watching a businessman take a dripping handful of pocket change and hurl it down a subway grate beside a homeless man. The coins bounced and clattered, disappearing into the humid dark. The rich man said, "Now you're having a shitty day too." But it is not a shitty day, and it will not be when I retrieve the bird and carry it—toes curling stiff from a shopping bag—to a houseless scrap of oak savannah, the very place the birdseed had drawn it from, and bury it in deeper snow, so that what was hoarded by one man may, by the thaw, be doled out again.
outputs.L2:
Jolted awake from its snow-day nap by the barking of a neighbor's dog, the bird knocked its vulture-like head and then failed to navigate the branches of the white pine, its wings too wide for the descent it had intended. Only some clumsy angel could say for certain whether death came before it struck the earth. But afterward, even the lowliest sinner could see the truth—those eyes hidden under naked, creased lids, the feet pulled up nearly level with the hands. I had enjoyed watching thistle and millet vanish under this creature out in the yard.

Now, as snowfall settles over feathers that will still shimmer come spring, my mind drifts to a memory: a well-dressed man scooping up a wet fistful of loose change and hurling it through a subway grate right next to a homeless person. The coins clinked and ricocheted before disappearing into the damp blackness below. The wealthy man declared that now the other man was having a lousy day too. Yet this isn't a lousy day, and it won't become one when I go collect the bird—its toes curling and rigid inside a shopping bag—and carry it to an ownerless patch of oak savannah, the very place the birdseed had lured it from, and bury it beneath deeper snow. That way, what one man kept for himself might, once the thaw arrives, be given out freely.
outputs.L3:
**The Fallen Bird**

A startled bird, buzzard-like in size and silhouette, misjudged the tangle of a white pine's limbs and could not thread its way through. It fell, and by the time it reached the ground it was already dead—though I cannot say with any certainty whether the fall itself killed it, or whether it had died mid-flight and only then dropped like a stone through the branches. That uncertainty stayed with me, a small unanswerable question left hanging in the cold air.

I came close and looked at it for a long while. Its eyes were hidden from me, as if it had turned inward at the last moment, and its feet were drawn up tight against its body in that curious way the dead have of folding themselves smaller. I recognized it, or thought I did. This was the same bird that had spent afternoons in the yard, the one beneath whom the scattered birdseed always seemed to vanish, grain by grain, until nothing was left but the memory of its hunger.

Snow had begun to gather on its feathers, dusting them white. And yet I knew that come spring those same feathers would have caught the light and turned iridescent, shimmering with colors that were now sealed away forever. Something about that thwarted promise—beauty that would never arrive—loosened a memory in me, an old scene I had witnessed and never quite forgiven.

I remembered a businessman and a homeless man on a city street. The homeless man had asked for whatever change might be spared, and the wealthy man, rather than simply refusing, chose cruelty. He dug the coins from his pocket and threw them down a subway grate, where they fell beyond any reach, and said with a thin smile that now the two of them were having a bad day together. It was a small act, and an enormous one—the deliberate destruction of something useful, the hoarding turned to spite, all so that nothing might be shared.

So I decided I would bury the bird in the oak savannah, where the grasses run long and the old trees stand spaced apart like patient witnesses. And as I imagined laying it in the earth, I found a kind of consolation. What one man clenches shut and refuses to release does not always stay withheld. The ground takes it in, the seasons turn, and eventually the thaw comes. What was hoarded is loosened; what was buried is given back. In the end, even the miser's coins and the fallen bird alike are surrendered to the slow generosity of the earth, released at last to be shared.
outputs.L4:
# The Buzzard in the Snow

The buzzard lay where it had fallen, a dark heap against the white expanse of the yard. Its wings were half-spread, as though it had tried in its last moments to catch the air and failed. Snow had begun to settle on the black feathers, softening the harsh geometry of a body that only days before had ridden the thermals high above the fields, patient and unhurried, waiting for the earth to offer up its dead.

I stood at the window a long while, watching it. There is something about a fallen scavenger that unsettles more than the death of a songbird or a deer. The buzzard is the one who cleans up after loss, who makes use of what the rest of us turn away from. To see it dead is to see the machinery of grief itself broken down, abandoned in the cold.

And for reasons I cannot fully explain, the sight called up a memory I had not thought of in years.

I was younger then, standing on a city sidewalk near the mouth of a subway grate. A man in an expensive coat—some businessman, hurried and glittering with the confidence of the well-fed—had passed a homeless man crouched against the wall. I remember thinking he might stop, might offer something. And he did stop. But what he did was worse than passing by. He reached into his pocket, pulled out a fistful of coins, and threw them down through the grate, into the darkness below, where no hand could ever reach them. He smiled as he did it. He wanted the poor man to see the money fall, to watch it disappear into a place where it could do no one any good.

That is cruelty of a particular kind—not the withholding of generosity, but its cruel parody. The performance of giving while ensuring nothing is given. The hoarding of even the act of charity, so that no warmth might escape into another's cold hands.

I have carried that memory like a stone. For years it seemed to me proof of something ugly at the center of things, and whenever I turned it over I could find no meaning in it, only the sour taste of a moment I would have called, if pressed, simply *shitty*—a small human evil, pointless and diminishing.

But standing there at the window, looking at the dead buzzard in the snow, I felt something shift.

I put on my coat and my boots and went out into the yard. The cold bit at my face. I knelt beside the bird and lifted it—heavier than I expected, and colder, the feathers stiff with frost. I held it against my chest and began to walk, out past the fence line, toward the wild oak savannah at the edge of the property, where the old trees stand scattered and bare against the sky, and no one comes.

I do not know entirely why I did this. I could have left the buzzard where it fell. The other scavengers would have found it, or the spring would have taken it back into the ground. But it seemed important to *choose* something, to make the moment mean what I wanted it to mean rather than what it threatened to.

I found a low place between the roots of the oaks and laid the bird down. Then I gathered snow over it, handful after handful, until it was covered—buried not in the frozen earth, which I could not have broken, but in the snow itself.

And here is what I understood as I worked: this was the opposite of the coins through the grate. The businessman had taken something and cast it where it could never be recovered, never shared, never do any good. But the snow is not the darkness beneath the grate. The snow is a promise. It does not keep what it holds forever. When the thaw comes—and it always comes—everything the snow has gathered will be released. The water will sink into the roots of the oaks. The body of the buzzard will return to the soil, to the grass, to the birds that come after. What I withheld from decay today, the season will give back tomorrow, freely, to everything that lives here.

I had thought I was performing a burial, an act of hoarding, of hiding something away. But I was doing the reverse. I was placing what I loved—this broken cleaner of the world—into the keeping of something that cannot help but give.

I stood and brushed the snow from my knees. Above me the bare oaks held up the gray sky. Somewhere in the frozen ground, the whole savannah was waiting, the way it waits every winter, to be generous again.

And I walked back toward the house, and the moment was no longer *shitty*. It was mine, and I had made it mean something, and it would keep on meaning it long after the snow was gone.
outputs.L5:
# A Sudden Awakening

The house was quiet when I first heard it—a soft, unexpected sound that left me **startled**, my heart pounding against my ribs. It came from **somewhere** deep within the shadows of the hallway, though I couldn't pinpoint exactly where.

I sat up straight, listening intently. Was it **any** cause for real concern, or simply my imagination running wild in the darkness? The mind has a curious way of transforming ordinary noises into something far more sinister when the lights go out.

Cautiously, I rose from my chair and made my way toward the source of the disturbance. Every creak of the floorboards made me flinch, and I felt **startled** all over again with each new sound. **Somewhere** in that endless corridor, something waited to be discovered.

Finally, I reached the kitchen and flipped on the light. There, perched on the counter, sat my cat—looking utterly unbothered by the chaos he had caused. A knocked-over glass explained everything. There wasn't **any** ghost, intruder, or mysterious force at play. Just a mischievous feline searching for **any** scrap of food he could find.

I laughed at my own foolishness. How quickly fear can grip us, and how easily it dissolves once we face the unknown. **Somewhere** in that moment, I learned a small lesson: not every sound in the night carries danger, and courage often means simply turning on the light.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about finding a dead bird after a snowstorm, weaving in a memory of witnessing an act of human cruelty in a city.
counterfactuals.output:
# Aftermath

The snow has stopped and left the world dressed in apology. I find it near the fence, a sparrow, wings folded as if still deciding whether to open. Frost has crept into the small architecture of its feathers. It weighs nothing now. It weighed nothing then, probably, in flight—but weight is not the same as absence.

I did not see it fall.

*

Years ago, in a city whose name I've let go soft, I watched a man strike another man for the change in his cup. It happened the way accidents happen, in the wrong order: the sound before the meaning, the meaning before the belief. Coins scattered across the sidewalk like something released. Nobody knelt to gather them. The struck man made himself smaller, an origami of survival, and I—I was late for something. I remember that. I remember I was late.

*

Here, the light comes back the way it always does, indifferent and gold, laying itself across the yard, across the bird, across my two useless hands. I could bury it. I could turn away. The snow offers no instruction. It has covered the coins, the cup, the city, the man who made himself small, the man who made him. It has covered everything and hidden nothing.

*

What I mean is: I keep a ledger I never asked to keep. What I mean is: some small deaths we witness only afterward, arriving always at the edge of the event, at the cooling of it, at the folded wings.

I lift the sparrow. It is the temperature of the morning. I hold what I could not prevent and did not cause, and this, too, is a kind of lateness—

to love a thing only once it can no longer flinch from being loved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, single-paragraph reflection on death, hoarding, and generosity, centered on a bird that died flying into a tree during a snow day.
counterfactuals.output: On the snow-hushed morning when the world went white and soft as forgetting, a small bird flew hard into the black arms of a tree and fell, a warm thing cooling in the cold, and I have been thinking ever since of how it carried nothing—no cache of seed hoarded against the lean months, no stored-up hours it might have spent more wisely, only the light architecture of hollow bones and the spent currency of a single flight given fully to the air—and I wonder at us, who gather and grip and pile our small hedgings against death as though the accumulation might buy us out of the falling, when the bird, who owned nothing, spent everything, seemed in its final unclenched openness to know the truer economy: that we come emptyhanded and leave the same, that the snow will cover the miser and the spendthrift alike, and that the only wealth we ever truly hold is the warmth we release while it is still ours to give, poured out like song into a morning that will not remember our names but will, for one bright unrepeatable instant, be filled.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a nature meditation that connects the burial of a dead hawk or buzzard to a scene of a wealthy man mocking a homeless person.
counterfactuals.output:
**Burial of a Buzzard**

I found it fallen at the field's brown edge,
wings spread as if still testing the last thermal,
the great hooked patience of its beak gone soft,
and something in me knelt without deciding to.

The grass was wet. I dug with a flat stone,
uncovering the small industrious dark—
the beetle-halls, the pale roots reaching down,
the earth's slow appetite that takes us all.

I laid it in. I thought of how it lived:
the long circling, the hunger held aloft,
the way it read the wind like a difficult psalm
and asked the sky for nothing but its due.

And then—because the mind will fold two things
together like the closing of a wing—
I remembered yesterday, the city corner,
the man asleep beneath his cardboard sky.

A well-dressed stranger passed him, laughing,
tossed a coin that missed, and did not stop to look,
the way you'd flick a leaf from a clean sleeve,
the way the living step around the dead.

There is a common ground beneath all this.
The buzzard and the beggar keep the same
appointment with the dark and patient loam
that does not check our pockets at the gate.

I pressed the soil down gently with both hands.
The wealthy man will come here too, someday,
his laughter emptied, his fine coat unbuttoned
by the same slow fingers that undo the hawk.

So let me learn to kneel while I am able,
to look at what has fallen, and stay looking—
for mercy is the only wealth we carry
past the field's edge, into the waiting ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, image-rich prose poem where the speaker discovers a dead bird in their yard and decides to bury it in oak savannah, contrasting winter scarcity with spring thaw.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Thaw Returns

I found it beneath the crabapple, a small grey commotion of feathers gone still, the junco's slate back dulled to the color of old snow crusted in the yard's north corners. Winter had been a long clenched fist—the feeders emptied, the suet cage swinging bare, the ground iron-locked and refusing every spade. For weeks the cold had been a kind of accountancy, subtracting the wrens, the field mice, the soft economies of warmth, until the world seemed pared to bone and blue shadow, to the bright arithmetic of survival where so many came up short.

So I carried it out to the savannah, that scatter-lot of ancient bur oaks standing wide-armed and separate in their acre of tallgrass, the sun-loving trees that keep their distance like old men who've learned the cost of crowding. Here the prairie had begun its slow undoing of the freeze. The earth gave. My spade broke through the frost-lace into the dark loam beneath, that first sweet reek of thaw-mud and root-rot and the green intention gathering underground—the sedges pushing up their pale spears, the pasque flowers furred and purple in the burn-scarred grass, the whole slow furnace of April relighting in the dirt.

I dug where the largest oak threw its noon shadow, into soil threaded with mycelium and the previous autumn's mast, the acorns split and sprouting, everything busy with its resurrection. And I laid the junco down in that opening dark, folded its wings against the coming season, covered it with the crumbling black bread of the ground.

Above me the branches ticked and dripped. A red-tailed hawk unspooled its cry across the warming blue. Somewhere the first returning bluebird tested the wet air, and the meltwater ran in bright threads through the grass, carrying winter off in pieces. I stood a while in that place of scattered trees and gathering green, holding the strange bright ledger where death is only the frost giving way, where the small grey debt of one cold morning is paid into the extravagant, indifferent, blooming account of spring.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something that begins with a bird startled from sleep and crashing into a white pine, then moves through themes of what is hoarded versus what is given away.
counterfactuals.output:
The Jay's Instruction

The jay came awake to nothing—
some dream-shape, a shadow the size
of an owl that wasn't there—
and launched itself blind into the white pine,
a soft catastrophe of feathers,
needles shaken loose, the whole tree
holding its breath in the dark.

Then stillness. The bird gripping bark,
heart going like a struggle,
while all around it the pine
gave off its resin smell, that sweetness
it never keeps, that leaks from every wound
it has, spending itself on the night air
freely, asking no one to notice.

I have watched the jays in autumn
bury their acorns, one by one,
into the earth's thousand pockets,
hoarding against the lean months,
and I have watched them forget—
so many of them forget—
where the treasure went,
until the forgetting becomes a forest,
oaks rising from the failed arithmetic
of appetite, the un-remembered gift.

So which is the bird's true work:
the keeping or the losing?
The frightened clutch at the branch,
or the branch itself, the pine
that clutches nothing, that offers up
its scent, its shade, its slow gold sap
to whatever passes?

Consider the difference between a fist
and an open hand—
how one holds warmth a little longer,
how one lets the light move through.

By morning the jay is gone,
about its burying and its forgetting,
and the tree stands where it stood,
having given all night what it could not save:
that fragrance, that dark generosity,
the wound that heals by opening,
the seed that only lives by being lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
